title: P-N Junction and Semiconductor Diodes
short_intro: A P-N junction is formed by joining p-type and n-type semiconductor materials, creating a localized depletion region devoid of mobile charge carriers. It exhibits asymmetric conductivity, allowing high current flow under forward bias and negligible current under reverse bias.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Qualitative understanding of p-type and n-type semiconductors, barrier potential, depletion region formation, forward and reverse biasing characteristics, and half-wave/full-wave diode rectification.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Quantitative analysis of depletion layer width, barrier potential derivation from doping concentrations, diode equation (Shockley equation), diffusion capacitance, transition capacitance, and Zener breakdown mechanisms.

prerequisites: Energy band theory in solids (valence, conduction, and forbidden energy gaps)
Intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors (Donor and acceptor impurity doping)
Fermi-Dirac distribution function and Fermi level position

concept_notes.heading: Formation of P-N Junction and Depletion Region
bullets: When p-type and n-type semiconductors are brought into contact, a concentration gradient causes electrons to diffuse from the n-side to the p-side and holes from the p-side to the n-side.
Diffusion of charge carriers leaves behind uncompensated immobile ionized donors (positive) on the n-side and ionized acceptors (negative) on the p-side near the interface.
The resulting space-charge region is called the depletion region, which establishes an internal electric field opposing further diffusion of majority carriers.

concept_notes.heading: Barrier Potential and Equilibrium
bullets: The accumulation of space charges sets up a potential barrier (V_0) across the junction that stops net diffusion current in thermal equilibrium.
Under equilibrium, the drift current due to thermally generated minority carriers exactly balances the diffusion current due to majority carriers.
The magnitude of the barrier potential depends on temperature and intrinsic carrier concentration as well as doping levels.

concept_notes.heading: Biasing Modes and V-I Characteristics
bullets: Under forward bias (p-side connected to positive terminal), the external field opposes the barrier potential, narrowing the depletion region and permitting large forward current.
Under reverse bias (n-side connected to positive terminal), the external field aids the barrier potential, widening the depletion region and allowing only a minute reverse saturation current (I_s).
At a critical high reverse voltage, avalanche breakdown or Zener breakdown occurs, causing a sharp increase in reverse current.

concept_notes.heading: Junction Capacitance Effects
bullets: Transition capacitance (C_T) or depletion layer capacitance arises from the change in stored space charge with applied reverse voltage, acting like a parallel plate capacitor.
Diffusion capacitance (C_D) arises from stored minority carrier charges in the neutral regions under forward bias conditions.
Both capacitances dictate the high-frequency response limitations of semiconductor diodes.

derivations.title: Barrier Potential Equation
derivations.conditions: Uniform doping, abrupt junction, thermal equilibrium at temperature T
steps: Write the expression for hole concentration on p-side and n-side using Boltzmann approximation: p_p = n_i exp((E_Fi - E_F)/kT) and p_n = n_i exp((E_Fn - E_F)/kT).
Relate the concentration ratio across the junction to the built-in potential V_0 using p_n = p_p exp(-qV_0 / kT).
Substitute donor concentration N_D and acceptor concentration N_A for majority carrier levels: p_p approx N_A and n_n approx N_D, keeping n_i^2 = N_A N_D.
Take the natural logarithm of both sides to isolate the potential V_0.

derivations.title: Depletion Layer Width Derivation
derivations.conditions: Abrupt asymmetrical p-n junction under thermal equilibrium
steps: Apply Poisson's equation in one dimension across the depletion width: d^2V / dx^2 = - \rho / \epsilon_s.
Express charge density rho as qN_D for x > 0 and -qN_A for x < 0, where x_n and x_p are the penetration depths into n and p sides.
Use charge neutrality condition: N_A x_p = N_D x_n.
Integrate the electric field and impose boundary conditions to find total depletion width W = x_p + x_n.

graphs_and_experiments.title: P-N Junction V-I Characteristic Curve
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A quadrant graph plotting forward voltage (V) versus forward current (mA) exponentially rising past cut-in voltage, and reverse voltage (V) versus reverse saturation current (\mu n/nA) showing sudden breakdown at V_z.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates non-linear, unidirectional conduction property of the diode with sharp breakdown under high reverse voltage.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked in identifying operating regions, calculating static/dynamic resistance, and explaining cut-in voltages for silicon (~0.7V) and germanium (~0.3V).

graphs_and_experiments.title: Energy Band Diagram of P-N Junction at Equilibrium
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Conduction and valence bands bending upward from p-side to n-side with a continuous horizontal Fermi level across the junction.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates the alignment of electrochemical potentials (Fermi levels) and the origin of the potential barrier inhibiting majority carrier drift.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in conceptual multiple-choice questions regarding band alignment under zero bias and external applied voltage.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Depletion Region Charge Density Profile
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A step function plot showing uniform negative charge density (-qN_A) from -x_p to 0 and positive charge density (+qN_D) from 0 to +x_n.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Visualizes the charge neutrality principle requiring total negative uncovered acceptor ions to equal total positive donor ions.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Basis for deriving electric field triangular distribution and potential parabolic profiles.

solved_numericals.question: A silicon diode operating at room temperature has a reverse saturation current of 20 nA. Calculate the forward diode current for a forward bias voltage of 0.6 V, assuming ideality factor eta = 1 and thermal voltage VT = 26 mV.
solution_steps: Identify given values: I_s = 20 \times 10^{-9} \text{ A}, V = 0.6 \text{ V}, V_T = \frac{kT}{q} = 0.026 \text{ V}, \eta = 1.
Substitute values into the Shockley diode equation: I = I_s \left( \exp\left(\frac{V}{\eta V_T}\right) - 1 \right).
Multiply by saturation current: I = 20 \times 10^{-9} \times 1.043 \times 10^{10} \approx 208.6 \text{ A (or dominant term approximation)}.

solved_numericals.question: For a germanium p-n junction at 300 K, the acceptor doping is N_A = 10^{17} \text{ cm}^{-3} and donor doping is N_D = 10^{14} \text{ cm}^{-3}. Given the intrinsic concentration n_i = 2.5 \times 10^{13} \text{ cm}^{-3} and thermal voltage V_T = 0.026 \text{ V}, calculate the built-in potential V_0.
solution_steps: Substitute given numbers: N_A = 10^{17}, N_D = 10^{14}, n_i = 2.5 \times 10^{13}.
Multiply by thermal voltage: V_0 = 0.026 \times 9.68 = 0.252 \text{ V}.

solved_numericals.question: A silicon step junction has relative permittivity \epsilon_r = 11.8, and total depletion width at zero bias is 0.5 \mu\text{m} with cross-sectional area 1 \text{ mm}^2. Find the transition capacitance C_T. (\epsilon_0 = 8.854 \times 10^{-12} \text{ F/m})

assumptions_and_limitations: The abrupt (step) junction approximation assumes an instantaneous transition from p-type to n-type doping, which is idealized compared to real diffused or ion-implanted junctions.
Boltzmann statistics are used instead of full Fermi-Dirac statistics, which holds true only for non-degenerate semiconductors where the Fermi level lies within the forbidden gap away from band edges.

common_misconceptions.wrong: No current flows through a p-n junction under thermal equilibrium.
common_misconceptions.correct: Net current is zero, but individual drift and diffusion currents flow and precisely cancel each other out.
common_misconceptions.why: Dynamic equilibrium implies opposing microscopic processes balance out on average.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The depletion region contains no charge carriers whatsoever.
common_misconceptions.correct: The depletion region is depleted of mobile majority carriers, but immobile ionized donor and acceptor ions are present.
common_misconceptions.why: Ions fixed to the crystal lattice create the space-charge region.

common_misconceptions.wrong: A reverse-biased diode has absolute zero current.
common_misconceptions.correct: A very small reverse saturation current (due to minority carrier thermal generation) constantly flows.
common_misconceptions.why: Minority carriers are swept across the junction by the electric field.

quick_revision: Depletion layer width decreases under forward bias and increases under reverse bias.
Shockley Diode Equation: I = I_s \left( \exp\left(\frac{qV}{\eta kT}\right) - 1 \right)
